questions.q: Where does SQL Pete's reward signal come from?
options: A human rater scoring each query by hand
Running the generated SQL and comparing its result set to the gold query's result set
A separate learned reward model, like in Project 2
The length of the generated SQL string
questions.explain: The reward is computed programmatically by executing the generated query against a sandboxed database and comparing result sets to the gold query.

questions.q: What happens to a generated query containing an UPDATE, DELETE, or DROP statement?
options: It is executed and then penalized if it causes damage
It is rejected before execution by a hard safety filter, scoring -1.0
It is executed only in read-only mode
It is automatically converted into a SELECT statement
questions.explain: Non-SELECT statements are caught by the safety filter and never reach the database at all, scoring -1.0.

questions.q: What reward does an exact result-set match receive?
questions.explain: An exact match between the generated query's result set and the gold query's result set scores +1.0.

questions.q: Why are result sets compared as unordered sets of rows rather than ordered lists?
options: Because SQL doesn't guarantee row order without an explicit ORDER BY, so ordering isn't part of correctness
Because ordered comparison is too slow to compute
Because the gold queries never return more than one row
Because Python sets are required by the transformers library
questions.explain: Without an ORDER BY clause, SQL doesn't guarantee row order, so penalizing a correct query for a different row order would be incorrect.

questions.q: Why does the safety rule reject disallowed statements BEFORE execution, rather than just scoring them -1.0 after running them?
options: Rejecting before execution is faster to code
A reward-optimizing policy will exploit any loophole, so the destructive action must be made structurally unreachable, not merely penalized after the fact
SQL engines cannot run UPDATE or DELETE statements at all
It has no real safety benefit either way
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as an alignment principle: don't just penalize a bad outcome, make it unreachable, since a reward-optimizing policy will find any exploitable loophole.
